draft.title: The cerebellum
card: The cerebellum is a structure at the back and base of the brain, below the cerebral cortex. It is part of the hindbrain.
It coordinates movement, so that actions are smooth and well timed. It does not start voluntary movements. It fine-tunes them.
It also helps keep balance and posture, so a person can stay upright and steady while they move.
It helps the brain learn motor skills, which are practised physical actions such as riding a bike. With practice, the movements become smoother and need less effort.
draft.remember: The cerebellum fine-tunes movement, balance and posture, and helps learn motor skills.

a.q: Which description best fits the role of the cerebellum?
opts: It smooths and times movements that are already underway
It decides which movement to make and starts it
It receives touch signals from the skin and body
It stores memories of past events for later recall
a.why: The cerebellum fine-tunes movement so that actions are smooth and well timed. It does not start voluntary movements, so the option about deciding and starting a movement is wrong, even though it sounds like movement control.

b.q: Priya is learning to ride a bike. After weeks of practice she stays upright and steers smoothly without thinking about it. Which part of the brain is most involved in this improvement?
opts: The cerebellum, which helps learn motor skills
The occipital lobe, which processes what she sees
The temporal lobe, which stores her memory of lessons
The frontal lobe, which starts every pedal movement
b.why: Riding a bike is a motor skill, and the cerebellum helps the brain learn it and smooth the movements with practice. The frontal lobe is tempting because it is involved in movement, but the card says the cerebellum fine-tunes movements rather than starting them.
b.clue: Which structure helps learn practised physical actions?

a.best: It smooths and times movements that are already underway

b.best: The cerebellum, which helps learn motor skills

The frontal lobe distractor uses the absolute 'every', which makes it easy to rule out. A student can match words rather than apply the idea.
